0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.name: Alawids
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.area: Morocco. Capitals: Fez, Meknes and Rabat
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.history:
The greatness of the Sa'dids was disproportionately linked to exceptionally favourable circumstances and the personalities of two sovereigns: 'Abd al-Malik and Ahmad al-Mansur.  
On the death of the latter (AH 1011 / AD 1603), the political and economic difficulties resurfaced, as did the unrest of the brotherhoods and the piracy that reinforced the breakdown of relations with Europe.  
The Alawid Sharifs, who held some power in Tafilalet, used their religious power and their skill as warriors and organisers to take control of eastern Morocco before taking Fez (1076 / 1666) and then Marrakesh (1079 / 1669).  
Mulay Isma'il, the most renowned of the sultans (1082–1139 / 1672–1727), consolidated the work of the founders of the dynasty and breathed new life into Moroccan civilisation. He fought the Turks and took the places still held by the Europeans on the Atlantic. However, this military power proved to be too costly and, after the death of Mulay Isma'il, Morocco fell into a deep political and economic crisis, which worsened the effect of the loss of revenues generated through privateering.  
After 30 years of chaos, Morocco experienced a spectacular recovery under Sidi Muhammad bin 'Abdallah (1170–1204 1757–90), who regained control of the army and the tribal administration and opened the country to the Atlantic by developing Tangiers and Casablanca and founding Essaouira, as well as re-establishing diplomatic and commercial links with Europe and even setting up relations with the USA. This recovery was cut short by a plague epidemic and a great famine, with the population plunging from five to three million between 1189 and 1214 / 1776 and 1800. The country became inward-looking and its weakness left it wide open to the vast European colonial movement.

12372d12-9b12-553c-861f-285f6d090ef6.name: Zirids
12372d12-9b12-553c-861f-285f6d090ef6.history:
The Fatimid Amir al-Mu'izz Ibn Badis al-Ziri, the new governor of Cairo, entrusted the Emirate of Ifriqiya \[Tunisia\] in AH 362 / AD 973, to one of his faithful lieutenants, the dignitary Yusuf ibn Ziri al-Sanhagi, advising him to adopt a policy of benevolence towards the towns and their inhabitants.  
Thus a dynasty was born that, at its peak, reigned over a vast area that stretched to central Maghreb. The Zirids had two administrative towns, Kairouan and then Mahdia, before returning to Monastir for their eternal rest. Under the Zirids, and in particular during the reign of al-Mu'izz (406–53 / 1016–62), Ifriqiya was a prosperous land, a fact recorded by many chroniclers. However, an event fraught with consequences jeopardised Zirid power and marked the history of medieval Ifriqiya: the Hilalian invasion launched in 443 / 1052 by the Caliph of Cairo to punish his vassal al-Mu'izz for having rejected the suzerainty of the Fatimids over his kingdom. The Zirids lost control of the country and withdrew to Mahdia, from where they were expelled in 542 / 1148 when the town was taken by the Normans.  
The Zirids made an important contribution to Ifriqiyan art, in particular:  
• The repair and decoration of the Great Mosque of Tunis, including the dome erected in 380 / 991 over the entrance of the prayer room, which brings together the most significant decorative elements of the time.  
• Decorative work on the Great Mosque of Kairouan, such as the painted ceilings and the addition of a *minbar* (pulpit) with high-quality wood carvings of plant motifs.  
• Expansions and conversions of other holy sites in places such as Monastir, Sousse and Sfax.  
• The construction of princely residences in the royal Fatimid city of Sabra al-Mansuriya at the gateway to Kairouan.  
• Fortifications in several of the county's coastal towns such as Monastir, where they are thought to be responsible for the al-Sayyida *ribat* (fortress), which was also their necropolis.

1d206364-a251-5fda-81dc-54a09e646e5e.name: Aghlabids
1d206364-a251-5fda-81dc-54a09e646e5e.history:
The spread of the Abbasid Empire and the re-establishment of the Umayyads in Al-Andalus and the Idrisids in Morocco, led the Abbasids to establish a local principality in North Africa to protect themselves against these rival powers surrounding their kingdom. In AH 184 / AD 800, Caliph Harun al-Rashid (169–93 / 786–809) gave Ifriqiya (Tunisia) to Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab (184–6 / 800–11), as a hereditary principality for him and his descendants to rule.  
Despite the many revolts they faced in their early days, the Aghlabids managed to establish their rule over Ifriqiya, pacifying the country and developing trade and communication. They rebuilt cities and villages, and constructed a series of fortresses along the Tunisian coast to defend the country from attack from their rivals or from the Byzantines.  
The Aghlabids controlled most of the islands in the western Mediterranean, including Sicily and Malta, and their influence extended as far as southern Italy. Ifriqiya experienced great prosperity under the Aghlabids, evident in the wealth of their architectural legacy, which included the Great Mosque of Kairouan and nearby reservoirs, and the Mosque of Zaytuna. Agriculture, weaving and ceramics also prospered, making Ifriqiya the main trade link between the Middle East and North Africa, and between Al-Andalus and Sudan.  
The inevitable fall of the Aghlabids came about mainly because of the brutality of the ruling prince Ibrahim II and the atmosphere of frivolity and profligacy that pervaded the reign of Ziyadat Allah III (290–6 / 903–9), which led the people of Ifriqiya to reject the Aghlabids and to refuse to support them against the spread of Shi'ism. Ifriqiya fell without a fight in 296 / 909 to the armies of Abu 'Abdallah al-Sana'ani, the founder of the Fatimid Dynasty, which went on to rule Egypt, Syria and Palestine.

29eaeead-971d-5ced-a2f3-a650a47f04ff.name: Safavids
29eaeead-971d-5ced-a2f3-a650a47f04ff.history:
The Safavid dynasty of Turkic origin was founded by the religious leader Safi al-Din Ardabili, who lived in Ardabil from 659 to 754 / 1252 to 1334. His religious order spread quickly in Anatolia, Iran and Iraq. The dynasty was supported by Tamerlane, the Ottomans and the Aq Qoyunlus and became more powerful especially during the reign of Hodja Ali, a grandson of Ardabili. When Shaykh Junayd, a grandson of Hodja Ali, interfered with the internal affairs of the Mamluks and the Qara Qoyunlus, relations with these powers deteriorated. Around the end of the AH 9th / AD 15th century, their relations with the Aq Qoyunlus also deteriorated and this led to the dissolution of the dynasty. However, the Safavids recovered quickly and Shah Isma'il established the Safavid State in 906 / 1501, with Tabriz as the capital.  
Joining forces with the Shi'a, the Safavids ruled over a vast area encompassing Iran, Iraq, Caucasia and east Anatolia. The Ottoman Sultan Selim I defeated Shah Isma'il at Çaldıran in 920 / 1514. Shah Isma'il was succeeded by his son Shah Tahmasp in 930 / 1524 and the capital was moved to Qazwin. After Shah Tahmasp, the Safavid State was ruled by Isma'il Mirza, Hamza Mirza, Shah Abbas, Sam Mirza, Abbas II, Shah Sulayman I, Shah Husayn, Tahmasp II and finally by Abbas III. Nadir Shah of Afshar origin brought the Safavid State to an end in 1150 / 1737 by conquering Iran.  
The Safavids built numerous monuments during their rule of approximately 250 years, especially in Iran. The palaces of Jihil Sütun and Hasht Bahisht, the Kiosk of Ali Kapı and the mosques of Masjid-i Shah and Shaykh Lutf Allah in Isfahan are among the major monuments of this period.

4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.name: Qing
4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.area: China, Taiwan, Tiber and Mongolia, as well as parts of central Asia
4ff94404-b748-5d95-93e3-648f784dd9ba.history:
The Qing dynasty was the last of the imperial dynasties of China. It was also the longest reigning dynasty, spanning the period from 1644 to 1912, and its rulers were renowned for their military prowess. The dynasty was also known as the Manchu dynasty as it was established by a Manchu clan (House of Aisin-Gioro), and half the royal officials were Manchu.  
  
The foundations of the Qing dynasty were laid when the Manchu people of northern China united against the Ming dynasty. Another group that went against the Ming dynasty was the Jurchen or the eastern barbarians. The group consisted of different tribes who inhabited the northeastern frontiers of the Ming empire. The Jurchen rose to power in the 1580s, led by a man named Nurhaci (also known as Nurgaci, 1559–1626), a Ming vassal who went on to unite all the Manchu clans. By 1583, after the death of his father and grandfather, Nurhaci emerged at 24 years old as the pre-eminent power in the region.  
  
Unlike the forebears of the Jurchen and other invaders and conquerors, Nurhaci’s tribesmen were not nomads. Their economy was dependent on agriculture, hunting and trade. In 1616, Nurhaci declared himself khan (“king”) of the Aisin dynasty. In a public document, he held the Ming rulers responsible for the deaths of his father and grandfather, calling them out for their abuse of power. The Ming dynasty responded by sending out a large number of militants against him, but this expeditionary force was defeated by a pan-Jurchen confederation led by Nurhaci.  
  
Nurhaci died in 1626, leaving his eighth son and heir, Hong Taiji (also known as Huang Taiji, 1626–43). Hong Taiji came to power as the descendent of his paternal grandfather, Giocangga. In 1616, Hong Taiji began driving out the Ming military from the Liaodong Peninsula. In 1629, he breached the Great Wall and occupied four Chinese cities: Luanzhou, Qian’an, Zunhua and Yongping. By 1636, he had established a functional government and went on to declare the formation of the “Great Qing” dynasty. Hong Taiji died on 21 September 1643, leaving behind a temporary power vacuum. After some negotiation it was decided that the emperor’s brother Dorgon (1612–50), together with the general named Jirgalang (1599–1655) would act as co-regents for Hong Taiji’s five-year-old son, Fulin. Fulin acceded to the throne in 1643 as the Shunzhi (“compliant rule”) emperor.  
  
From the 1750s to 1790s, the Qianlong emperor extended Qing control into the interior territories of Asia. At its height, the empire ruled over almost all of today’s mainland China, including Hainan, Taiwan, Mongolia, parts of Manchuria and northwest China. The Qing rulers maintained their Manchu custom and followed Tibetan Buddhism. The dynasty reached its peak in the 18th century but gradually deteriorated due to challenges from abroad, revolts within the kingdom, population growth, a disordered economy and corruption. The Qing dynasty was finally overthrown with the formation of the Republic of China in 1912.  
  
Bibliography  
• Smith, Richard J., The Qing Dynasty and Traditional Chinese Culture, Washington, DC: Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 2015.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.name: Nasrids
ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.history:
When the Almohad Caliph al-Ma'mun, enthroned in Seville in AH 624 / AD 1227, returned to Morocco, a member of the vizier Banu al-Ahmar family, Muhammad bin Yusuf bin Nasr, proclaimed himself king (627 / 1230) founding the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled Granada until 897 / 1492.  
He stayed in power by paying an annual tribute to the king of Castile and assisted passively in the breathtaking progress of the Christian Reconquista, with the surrender of Córdoba (633 / 1236), Jaen and Arjona (643 / 1246), and Seville (645 / 1248).  
Thanks to their plotting and dealing and the occasional military support of the Marinids, the Nasrids experienced a veritable golden age, the most stunning examples of which being the Alhambra and the Generalife. This splendour lasted until 886 / 1482 when Boabdil (Abu 'Abdallah) overthrew his father but failed to contain the Reconquista. Malaga fell in 892 / 1487; Baeza and Almeria in 894 / 1489, among other places. He ended up capitulating, and the Catholic kings entered Granada on 2 January 1492, closing the book on the epic that was 'al-Andalus'.  
The existence of al-Andalus as a Muslim political entity lasted nearly 800 years, but the Reconquista, which began in 722 (Battle of Pelayo / Covadonga) lasted nearly 900, continuing to 1610 with successive waves of expulsions of 'moriscos'.  
However, although al-Andalus ceased to exist as a political entity, its cultural and artistic influence lived on in Spain, where Mudejar art conditioned architectural thought until the 18th century, and in Morocco, where Hispano-Moorish architecture and craftsmanship successfully combined Hispano-Visigothic art with traits of the Muslim West and the Berbers, the latter having survived through the Sharif dynasties.

c86e40a5-f47d-5f06-8a89-26f52f632eb0.name: Fatimids
c86e40a5-f47d-5f06-8a89-26f52f632eb0.history:
The assassination of Caliph 'Ali in the Iraqi city of Kufa, and of Imam Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, at Karbala, gave rise to Shi'ism, which is based on a belief in the right of the descendants of Muhammad to assume the caliphate. Opposed by the Umayyads and then the Abbasids, the movement nonetheless spread quickly through the Muslim world to reach the Maghreb, from where the Shi'a Muslims decided to conquer the great caliphate of the Muslim world. Brought to power by the missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, Imam al-Mahdi ousted the Aghlabid Dynasty in AH 297 / AD 910 before taking Tunisia, Libya, eastern Algeria and Sicily.  
In 358 / 969, strengthened by the country's economic prosperity and stability, the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz (r. 341–64 / 953–75) attempted to reconquer the East and was victorious in Egypt, leaving Ifriqiya \[Tunisia\] to the Zirids, who quickly abandoned Shi'ism for Sunnism, an act violently repressed by the Hilalian tribes that attacked the country.  
The new Fatimid capital, Cairo, became the cradle of a brilliant civilisation, bolstered by territorial conquests in Syria and Palestine. Until Salah al-Din (Saladin) finally seized power from them in 566 / 1171, the Fatimid caliphs promoted urban development, the sciences, art and literature.  
The Fatimids founded several towns including Mahdiyya and Sabra al-Mansuriyya in Ifriqiya, Achir in central Maghreb and Cairo in Egypt. In accordance with their philosophy and faith, towns were no longer organised around the mosque, but around the palace of the caliph as a symbol of power. Porticoes also began to appear in the courtyards of mosques with offset corridors in prayer rooms for the glorified procession of the caliph.  
The sciences, art, mathematics, medicine and exegesis developed spectacularly under the Fatimids, as did applied arts and crafts. Glass and ivory figures of humans and animals remain the most well known.

cc058ff2-1729-58a0-be91-e1ac612c1fe2.name: Mamluks
cc058ff2-1729-58a0-be91-e1ac612c1fe2.history:
For more than two and a half centuries the Mamluk Sultanate was one of the major powers in the lands of Islam and indeed the wider world. The literal meaning of the word *mamluk* in Arabic is 'owned', but in common use it donates a military slave, and it was indeed military slaves, acquired from the Eurasian steppes through the Black Sea ports by the last Ayyubid sultan Najm al-Din, who were to launch the Mamluk regime and carry it to unforeseen glory.  
*Mamluk* slaves came from different ethnic groups, but the majority were Turks and Circassians from the Caucasus. Acquired to become loyal fighters for the cause of the sultan, they were instructed in the principles of Islam and learnt extensive cavalry skills and fighting techniques. Their superior military abilities soon enabled the Mamluks to establish their own rule and build an empire that was to control Egypt, the Levant and the holy Muslim cities in Hijaz for well over two centuries.  
The Mamluk sultans came to be distinguished in two main lines: the Bahri Mamluks, so called because these guards of the Ayyubids originally had their barracks on the island of al-Rawda \[Rhoda\] in the Nile (al-Bahr), ruled from AH 648 to 792 / AD 1250–1390. The Burji Mamluks, named because Sultan Qalawun had quartered his guards in the towers (*burg*) of Cairo, ruled from 784 to 923 / 1382–1517.  
Not only did the Mamluks repel the Mongol threat once and for all by a decisive defeat at 'Ayn Jalut in Palestine in 658 / 1260, but they also fiercely attacked the Crusaders' castles in Palestine and eventually expelled them totally from Akko in Palestine in 690 / 1291. On the diplomatic and economic fronts, the Mamluk Sultanate built strong ties with all the important Muslim powers as well as the Far East, Byzantium, France, Castile, Sicily, Genoa and Venice. Cairo became the trade hub of the world, and the exotic goods from East and West exchanged there provided ample inspiration for local artisans and were reflected in the work they produced.  
The Mamluks were outstanding defenders of Islam and committed protectors of its Holy Cities. They restored the Caliphate in Cairo in 659 / 1261 after the devastation of its original seat in Baghdad and devoted much of their interest to the building of splendid mosques, *madrasas* (religious schools) and *waqfs* (religious foundations) in cities such as Cairo, Jerusalem, Aleppo and Damascus. The best artists and craftsmen were called upon to provide these buildings with calligraphic and geometric decoration, with religious furniture, Qur'ans, carpets and utensils. Patronage was also given to objects designed to reflect the official and private splendour of the Mamluk sultan and his court.  
The decline of Mamluk supremacy came with the discovery of new trade routes around the Cape of Good Hope and the expansion of Ottoman power, which eventually was to extinguish the Mamluk Sultanate in 923 / 1517.

d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.name: Qajar
d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.area: Persia (Iran), Georgia and Armenia (subsequently lost to the Russian Protectorate and ultimately the British Empire)
d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.history:
The Qajars were of Turkoman origin, based near Astarabad in northeastern Iran. The Qajar dynasty ruled Iran from 1785 to 1925. During this time, the Qajars unified Iran, promoting and encouraging new innovations in technology (such as the telegraph and railroads). The arts also flourished under their reign; photography and lithography, along with innovative forms of portraiture and oil painting brought from the West, were enthusiastically adopted by artists and patrons alike. In the 140 years that the Qajar dynasty ruled, Iran was transformed from feuding tribal confederations to a centralized monarchy and finally to a constitutional parliament. In the historical consciousness of the people, the Qajars invoked the glorious Safavid era with all its might and splendour.  
  
The first Qajar shah was Agha Mohammad Shah (1795–98). His main concern at the time of his rule was to consolidate the country’s position against its opponents, the Zands of Shiraz (1750–94). He defeated the last Zand prince, Lotf Ali Khan. Finally, Agha Mohammad Khan was assassinated by one of his attendants in May 1796 and was succeeded by his nephew, Baba Khan, who was crowned and given the name Fath ‘Ali Shah.  
Fath ‘Ali Shah ruled from 1797 to 1834. He worked on redefining the Qajar imperial image and distinguishing it from that of his predecessors. In the 37 years that Fath ‘Ali Shah reigned, he united his fellow citizens and worked to better the growing administration of the country. This was the time of the first Russo-Persian war, when Iran’s territories of Georgia and Azerbaijan were taken by rivals. The political situation with Russia and Britain was not always agreeable. A second Russo-Persian war began in the summer of 1826 in the Caucasus where Muslims fought against the Russians. After this war Iran was able to recover all its lost territories.  
  
Fath ‘Ali Shah died in 1834 and was succeeded by his grandson, Mohammad Shah (1834–48). However, Mohammad Shah’s accession led to a feud with two of his uncles, Zel al-Soltan, governor of Tehran, and Farman Farma in Fars. Each of them believed that they deserved to be successors of Fath ‘Ali Shah. Russia and Britain recognized Mohammad Shah as the successor, and he was helped and advised by Abol Qasem Qa’em Maqam, his father’s minister. He was ultimately was crowned sovereign in a ceremony held in Tehran. Mohammed Shah died in September 1848. His reign had been far from peaceful as most of it was spent struggling with Britain. He was succeeded by his son, Naser al-Din Mirza.  
  
At the age of 17 years, Naser al-Din Shah (1848–96) acceded to the throne. He initiated change and modernized the capital city of Tehran. His guide was Mir Taqi Khan Amir Nezam (later known as Amir Kabir) who served as Sadr Azam. Amir Kabir implemented reforms to modernise, develop and reform the state. He also undertook to reform the financial and military systems. His most notable achievement, however, was the establishment of Dar al-Funun (Abode of Sciences), one of the first schools in Iran to be based on a Western model of teaching. He considered it a good training ground for future civil servants and military men.  
  
After the death of Naser al-Din Shah, Mozaffar al-Din Shah (1896–1906) became the new sovereign at 43 years of age. He was known as a weak ruler and was considered more lenient with his subjects compared to his father. One of his achievements was issuing the firman, a royal edict stating that he granted a Majles (consultative assembly) and that elections would be held. The elections in Tehran were speedily performed and the first Majles was opened by Mozaffar al-Din Shah on 7 October 1906. The first act of the Majles was to prepare a constitution - a first in Iranian history. This was accomplished and signed by the ruler Mozaffar al-Din Shah five days before his death in February 1907. He was succeeded by his son, Mohammad Ali Shah.  
  
Mohammad Ali Shah (1907–09) was 35 years old at the time of his accession. He was raised by a Russian tutor, which made him unpopular with Iranian nationalists who later turned against him. The Shah attempted a coup d’état in December 1907, which failed. He was criticized by officials and the general public at the Majles. In July 1907, he abdicated the throne and left it to his 12-year-old son, Ahmad Mirza.  
  
When Ahmad Shah (1909–25) became the Qajar sovereign, the northern region of the country was under occupation; the Russo-British agreement of 1907 meant that the ministers of both countries interfered in the internal affairs of Iran, particularly in designating the membership of the cabinets. During the First World War (1914–18) Iran was besieged by Russian, British and Ottoman troops. Ahmed Shah could not recover from this setback. With a coup d'état in February 1921, Reza Khan (later known as Reza Shah Pahlavi) was elected to take the place of Ahmed Shah, who was deposed by the Majles.  
  
Bibliography  
• Algar, Hamid, Religion and State in Iran 1785-1906 - The Role of the Ulama in the Qajar Period, Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, 1980.  
• Daryaee T. (ed), The Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, UK: Oxford University Press, 2012.  
• Gleave, Robert, Religion and Society in Qajar Iran, UK: Routledge Curzon Press, BIPS Persian studies series, 2005.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

f108d67e-06c0-5769-ad8d-5e30d2542f68.name: Almohads
f108d67e-06c0-5769-ad8d-5e30d2542f68.area: North Africa and Spain. Capital: Marrakesh
f108d67e-06c0-5769-ad8d-5e30d2542f68.history:
The decline and fall of the Almoravid empire was essentially caused by popular uprisings against the nepotism and corruption of rulers who had abandoned themselves to the luxury and indifference of palace life.  
The Almohads (al-Muwahidun: the unitarians), a reformist Berber clan descended from the High Atlas to denounce the unholy Almoravids, took Marrakesh in AH 541 / AD 1147 and their leader, 'Abd al-Mu'min, took the title Amir al-Muminin.  
His grandson, Ya'qub al-Mansur, who won a crucial victory over the Iberian armies at Alarcos in 597 / 1195, was a great builder and patron, and he led the empire to its political, economic, intellectual and artistic high point.  
The Almohads succeeded in unifying a huge empire covering the entire Muslim West (North Africa from the Atlantic to Gabes) and Muslim Spain, before beginning to decline in 608 / 1212 with a heavy defeat at the hands of the Christian armies at Las Navas de Tolosa (Jaen). They had intended to establish a new capital, but the death of Ya'qub al-Mansur (595 / 1199) and the decline of the dynasty prevented the completion of Ribat al-Fath (Rabat).  
The buildings erected by the Almohads, both in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, are evidence of a continuous concern for grandeur and sobriety with their huge ramparts, monumental gateways, majestic minarets and fine decorative motifs.

f1abebd4-ee55-56ed-a5f8-6d9290aff818.name: Ilkhanids
f1abebd4-ee55-56ed-a5f8-6d9290aff818.area: Persia, Iraq, eastern and central Anatolia.
f1abebd4-ee55-56ed-a5f8-6d9290aff818.history:
The Ilkhanid state was founded by Hülagü \[Hülegü or Hulaku\], brother of the great Mongolian Khan Mengü \[Möngke\]. Mengü ascended the throne in AH 651 / AD 1253 and sent his brother Hülagü to Iran. Hülagü founded his state in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Anatolia, which had come under Mongolian rule following the Battle of Kösedağ (640 / 1243).  
Hülagü, a Buddhist, launched many campaigns in order to strengthen the Mongolian rule in western Asia and conquered Iran and Azerbaijan in 654 / 1256, Baghdad in 656 / 1258 (resulting in the fall of the Abbasid Empire and Caliphate) and Aleppo in 657 / 1259. However, he failed to conquer Damascus. The Mamluks in Egypt and the Altınordu \[Golden Horde\] states joined forces against the Ilkhanids.  
Abaqa, who was also a Buddhist, succeeded his father Hülagü (d. 663 / 1265). He continued the conflict against the Mamluks and plundered Syria and Anatolia. His son Ahmad Han, who succeeded him, was a Muslim and wanted to establish good relations with the Muslim states. But Ahmad could not hold power for long and died in 683 / 1284 following years of fighting for the throne with his brother Arghun. Arghun held power until 690 / 1291 and continued his fights against the Muslim states. He was succeeded shortly by Gaykhatu and then by Ghazan Mahmud Han in 694 / 1295. The Ilkhanids converted to Islam during Ghazan Mahmud's reign.  
Ghazan was succeeded by his son Khudabanda Uljaytu Han (r. 702­–15 / 1303–16), who favoured the Shi'a and extended the Ilkhanid territory, conquering Khurasan and Herat. He was succeeded by his very young son Abu Sa'id Bahadur Han, who favoured the Sunni. Bahadur appointed Choban Noyan as vizier but soon fell out with him. Choban Noyan was murdered in 728 / 1327, which led to uprisings in the Ilkhanid army. The uprisings ended when Bahadur died in 736 / 1335 and the state fell and new states emerged: Amir Choban Oghullari in Azerbaijan, Shaykh Hasan in Baghdad and the Eretna Emirate in eastern Turkey.

f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.name: Ottomans
f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.area: Anatolia, Balkans, Arab lands from Iraq to Algeria
f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.history:
The Ottoman Dynasty, which ruled for more than 600 years over the eastern Mediterranean, represents an important period of world history in the region and beyond. The Ottoman Emirate, one of the emirates of western Anatolia, burst onto the stage of history in AH 698 / AD 1299 with Osman \['Uthman\] Bey, who quickly extended his territories by signing treaties with other emirates, or by declaring war on them, during a chaotic period for Anatolia in the AH 8th and 9th / AD 14th and 15th centuries.  
The Ottomans also survived the Mongols and established themselves as a considerable force in the region. With their army and the invincible armada of the navy, the Ottomans took Istanbul in AH 856 / AD 1453 and created an empire. Their supremacy reached its peak during the reign of Süleyman the Legislator (also known as the Magnificent), AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66, when their empire stretched to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.  
With its abundance of different influences, the Ottomans built a cultural empire that strove to establish, defend and promote interaction between the elements that made up its ethnic and religious mosaic. Its eastern character dominated until the AH 12th / AD 18th century, when political changes made it susceptible to winds of change from the West, which really took hold in the AH 13th / AD 19th century.  
During its ascendancy the empire managed to forge effective relationships with other states, but during its decline, pressures from outside seriously weakened the empire and led to its eventual destruction. Furthermore, the reforms of the AH 13th / AD 19th century never really took hold, and enlightened reformists were often beaten down by religious dogmatism. During this process the subjection of the people to the absolute power of the sultan, which retarded the emergence of critical voices, and the limited development of education, contributed to this 'global empire' taking its place in the pages of history.
